papers.title: Simulating Patient Resistance in silico: Evaluating Concepts in Rare Diseases using Patient Agents with Limited Rationality
papers.summary: The evaluation of new medical concepts and digital health devices for rare diseases is hampered by the scarcity and vulnerability of real-world patient cohorts.Synthetic sampling (Silicon Sampling) using personas driven by large language models (LLMs) offers a promising digital evaluation framework, but one that is biased by 'algorithmic perfection': over-rational decision-making, omniscience via retrieval-from-sources (RAG) and sycophancy.This article establishes a methodological framework based on the meta-ergonomics of falsification and the Adversarial Cognitive Twin (ACT) architecture.Rather than increasing the persona's theoretical intelligence, we propose to falsify the synthetic agent by injecting it with calibrated cognitive impairments, semantic entropy, reduced user knowledge bases and multiagent contradiction loops.This methodological constraint enables the simulation of mental load, doubts and user resistance -characteristics specific to clinical reality.An experimental benchmarking protocol based on secondary data enables the measurement of error alignment and the rate of compliance inhibition.This work defines a robust and ethical framework for use, compliant with the requirements of the EU AI Act, positioning the constrained persona as a filter for user resistance prior to in vivo clinical research.

papers.title: Purpose-Bounded Context Exchange in Enterprise Agentic AI Systems: An Inter-Module Information Contract Architecture
papers.summary: Enterprise agentic AI systems exchange contextual information across functional modules, creating governance challenges when information crosses operational and organizational boundaries. This study distinguishes organizational governance boundaries from information exchange boundaries and proposes an Inter-Module Information Contract (IMIC) architecture for purpose-bounded context exchange. IMIC evaluates provenance, semantic and temporal validity, permitted information scope, and applicable originating constraints before downstream execution, independently of language-model reasoning. We compare IMIC with full-context sharing, reduced-context sharing, and strengthened structured handoff. In a deterministic benchmark of 32 synthetic conditions, joint correctness is achieved in 3, 10, 28, and 32 cases, respectively. The four differences between strengthened structured handoff and IMIC arise from conditions testing onward-transfer permission, recipient, purpose, and field scope. A downstream integration experiment evaluates 14 selected conditions across four local language models and three seeds, yielding 168 case–model–seed blocks and 672 method-level records. IMIC achieves correct exchange actions and information boundaries in all 168 blocks and joint correctness in 165 across four local LLMs and three seeds. Three permitted executions produce incorrect downstream responses de

papers.title: The Rise of Language Models in Mining Software Repositories: A Survey
papers.summary: The Mining Software Repositories (MSR) field focuses on analyzing the rich data contained in software repositories to derive actionable insights into software processes and products. Mining repositories at scale requires techniques capable of handling large volumes of heterogeneous data, a challenge for which language models (LMs) are increasingly well-suited. Since the advent of Transformer-based architectures, LMs have been rapidly adopted across a wide range of MSR tasks. This article presents a comprehensive survey of the use of LMs in MSR, based on an analysis of 177 papers. We examine how LMs are applied, the types of artifacts analyzed, which models are used, how their adoption has evolved over time, and the availability of supplementary materials and tools supporting reproducibility and reuse. Building on this analysis, we propose a taxonomy of LM applications in MSR, identify key trends shaping the field, and highlight open challenges alongside actionable directions for future research.

papers.title: Uncertainty-Guided Counterfactual Sensor Selection and Safety-Gated Recognition for Autonomous Sensing Agents in IoT Systems
papers.summary: Autonomous IoT systems rely on distributed sensing, but sensor faults and communication loss can leave multichannel evidence incomplete or unreliable. Their agents must therefore classify measurements, assess evidence sufficiency, select a sensor to reacquire, and hand off unsafe decisions. We formulate counterfactual sensing: a degraded window defines the factual state, each candidate restoration defines a controlled alternative, and a pre-request utility model estimates loss reduction. Physics-Guided Invariant-Kinematic Fusion (PGIK-Fusion) constructs class evidence, while calibrated risk and cost-sensitive utility select acceptance, sensor request, or handoff from factual information. On the Logistic Activity Recognition Challenge dataset, PGIK-Fusion achieves 0.768 accuracy and a macro-averaged F1 score (Macro-F1) of 0.696, exceeding extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost)--one-dimensional convolutional neural network (1D-CNN) fusion by 2.49 and 2.00 percentage points, respectively. Across seven predefined degradation conditions on held-out subjects, the policy reduces unsafe acceptance from 33.0% to 13.8%; relative to an action-rate-matched random policy, it raises automation accuracy by 18.5 percentage points and lowers expected cost by 24.7%. In the auxiliary within-event wind-turbine study, PGIK-Fusion reaches 0.975 Macro-F1, improves on XGBoost--1D-CNN by 1.17 percentage p

papers.title: TeamGym: A Gym for Team Decision-Making by AI Agents with Distributed Information
papers.summary: Many real-world decisions require teams to integrate information distributed across participants. Yet AI agents are still primarily trained and benchmarked in isolation. We introduce TeamGym, an environment for evaluating and training language model-based agents on team decision-making problems constructed from real-world legal, finance, medical, and software engineering corpora. TeamGym introduces a method to identify a minimal set of facts, each element of which is necessary and all of which are collectively sufficient for a correct final decision, which we call pivotal information. This enables TeamGym to both control the distribution of pivotal information and track how well agents identify and integrate pivotal information when making team decisions. Examining 8 language models on 12 source corpora, we find that current AI agents often fail to effectively share information: Distributing pivotal information across participants lowers success rate by 22.9 percentage points on average relative to giving the same information to a single model (a communication gap). We also document that participants do not effectively retrieve decision-relevant information on their own: A team's success rate is lowered by a further 19.9 points when participants must identify and extract pivotal information from source material rather than receiving it directly (a retrieval gap). To help remedy

papers.title: Remembering Is Not Enough: Refining Memories and Learning When to Use Them in Multi-Agent Systems
papers.summary: Memory helps LLM-based multi-agent systems reuse experience, but stored advice can be flawed or applied in the wrong situation. Team-level success or failure alone cannot reliably show whether a memory needs correction or should not have been used. We propose DiscernMem, a training-free framework that improves both memory quality and memory use. To improve quality, Defect-Aware Memory Refinement (DMR) compares team executions with a single memory and with no memory, diagnoses rule defects, and tests repairs on current and earlier tasks to guard against losing previously useful behavior. To guide appropriate use, Boundary-Learning Meta-Memory (BLM) records each memory's past uses and effects, learning when its owner role should apply or avoid it based on task context and incoming messages. Together, these components help teams correct flawed experience while retaining useful rules that were applied incorrectly. Experiments with Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 on four benchmarks show that DiscernMem achieves the highest average score on AutoGen, CAMEL, and MacNet, exceeding the strongest reported baselines by 0.51-4.32 points. It leads on code generation and symbolic planning across all three systems, including a PDDL score of 37.71 versus 28.48 on CAMEL.

papers.title: Design and Evaluation of an Artificial Intelligence–Based Model for Predicting Twelfth-Grade Students’ Mathematics Performance Based on Individual, Educational, and Learning Technology Factors
papers.summary: Purpose: This study aimed to design and evaluate an artificial intelligence–based model for predicting the mathematics performance of twelfth-grade experimental sciences students based on individual, educational, and learning technology factors. Methods and Materials: This applied, quantitative, cross-sectional, and predictive study was conducted among twelfth-grade experimental sciences students in Isfahan, Iran. A total of 187 questionnaires were distributed, and after removing incomplete, inconsistent, and invalid records, data from 84 students were retained for analysis. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire assessing individual factors, educational conditions, and learning technology variables, together with students’ recorded mathematics scores. The dataset was divided into training and testing subsets, and repeated five-fold cross-validation was used for internal model development. Multiple linear regression, ridge regression, lasso regression, elastic net regression, decision tree regression, random forest regression, gradient boosting regression, and support vector regression were compared. Model performance was evaluated using mean absolute error, root mean squared error, and the coefficient of determination. Findings: Previous mathematics achievement had the strongest positive correlation with current mathematics performance, followed by mathematics se

papers.title: Automated creation of source code variants of a cryptographic hash function implementation using generative pre-trained transformer models
papers.summary: Generative pre-trained transformers (GPTs) are a type of large language machine learning model that are unusually adept at producing novel, and coherent, natural language. However, GPT model outputs in general are stochastic and not always correct. For programming languages, the exact specification of the computer code, syntactically and algorithmically, is strictly required in order to ensure the security of computing systems and applications. Therefore, using GPT models to generate computer code poses an important security risk—while at the same time allowing for potential innovation in how computer code is generated. This study examines GPT model outputs of novel and correct, and notably very insecure, versions of implementations of the cryptographic hash function SHA-1. The GPT models Llama-2-70b-chat-hf, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.1, and zephyr-7b-alpha are used. The GPT models are prompted to re-write each function using a modified version of the localGPT framework to provide word embedding context of the full source code and header files to the model, resulting in over 150, 000 function re-write GPT output text blocks, approximately 50, 000 of which were able to be parsed as C code and subsequently compiled. The generated code is analyzed for being compilable, correctness of the algorithm, memory leaks, compiler optimization stability, and character distance to the reference

papers.title: Age-related changes in memory for gist and details: New perspectives on the representational quality of episodic memory.
papers.summary: Substantial heterogeneity in adult age-related declines in episodic memory within and across tasks and individuals has prompted extensive theoretical debate about the source of these variations.Today, many theories assume that age-related changes in the representational fidelity of memory and the degree to which a test demands the retrieval of specific details of past experiences underlie much of this variability.This special issue of Psychology and Aging presents 19 contributions from researchers from around the world that together aim to enrich our understanding of the representational basis of age-related memory change.These contributions explore several interrelated themes related to measuring, predicting, and, at times, counteracting age-related declines in memory specificity while extending representational accounts to new tasks, more naturalistic contexts, and populations spanning the adult lifespan as well as individuals with neurocognitive impairment.The breadth of coverage spans multiple research domains with rich histories in the field of cognitive aging, including recognition memory, autobiographical memory, event memory, decision making, comprehension, and computational modeling.Collectively, the diversity of questions posed by the articles and the varied methods they advance to addressing them highlight the value of integrating findings across different research t

papers.title: Bounds on user repair after context loss in AI handoffs
papers.summary: Long-running artificial intelligence (AI) conversations can lose permissions, commitments, or goals when they cross model and context boundaries. This theoretical paper asks when bounded system recovery makes external user repair necessary. We propose a provenance-bearing register of governing constraints and derive a lower bound combining graded continuity shortfall with unrecoverable hard constraints. The bound requires valid recovery ceilings and need not be achievable by an actual policy. A joint feasible-recovery formulation characterizes the minimum repair within the model, while a finite-action formulation handles discrete retrieval, model choices, and complementary actions. Smooth resource allocation is treated as a special case. An author-constructed coding-assistant example illustrates how broad recall and constraint preservation can disagree. A synthetic sensitivity analysis varies weights, thresholds, hard status, and recovery access; it establishes conditional robustness within the example, not classification accuracy on real conversations. Supplementary materials provide the calculation code, a coding manual, a weight-elicitation instrument, and a prospective validation protocol. No independent rater study, model benchmark, or human-participant evaluation is reported. The contribution is a testable account of how a declared architecture can externalize continuity

papers.title: TACO-Graph: Automated Construction of Text-Atributed Graphs
papers.summary: Graph-structured representations of text data have become foundational across machine learning, yet it remains unclear how to systematically construct a graph from a given dataset for a target task. Choices about which entities become nodes, which relationships become edges, and what text each node contains can substantially affect downstream performance. In practice, finding optimal constructions often requires expert knowledge or manual trial and error. We introduce TACO-Graph, a decision tree framework for learning which graph construction choices are most effective for a given dataset and task. Specifically, we focus on text-attributed graphs (TAGs) constructed from multi-attribute tabular data. TACO-Graph enumerates valid TAG representations, scores each using fast proxy evaluation on small representative subsets, and trains an interpretable decision tree on those scores. Across five datasets spanning citation networks, product reviews, and bibliographic relationships, our decision trees predict construction quality on separately drawn evaluation samples with mean Spearman $ρ$ above $0.9$ for node classification and above $0.8$ for GraphRAG retrieval. Our trees systematically identify which constructions perform better across both GNN and GraphRAG tasks, and the full pipeline is released as an open-source library to support evaluation on new tasks and datasets at https://g

papers.title: Narrative theory-driven LLM methods for automatic story generation and understanding: a survey
papers.summary: Abstract Applications of narrative theories using large language models (LLMs) deliver promising methods in automatic story generation and understanding tasks. Our survey examines how natural language processing (NLP) research uses LLM methods to engage with diverse concepts from narrative studies. We use established distinctions from narratology to categorise ongoing efforts and discover the following: (a) narrative texts come from diverse sources beyond just literature, (b) theoretical synthesis and validation are potential outcomes, (c) generation tasks lag behind understanding in several ways: theoretical application, post-training methods, exploring non-fiction narratives and addressing narrative levels beyond fabula and discourse. For future directions, instead of the pursuit of a single, generalised benchmark for ‘narrative quality’, we believe that progress can benefit from efforts that focus on the following: defining and improving theory-based metrics for individual narrative attributes; continue conducting large-scale, theory-driven literary/social/cultural analysis; generating narratives in situated contexts; and continuing experiments where outputs can be used to validate or refine narrative theories. This work provides a contextual foundation for more systematic and theoretically informed narrative research in NLP by providing an overview to ongoing research effor

papers.title: An agentic framework for intelligent clinical laboratory medicine
papers.summary: Clinical laboratory medicine is fundamental to healthcare yet remains an underrecognized frontier for artificial intelligence. We propose LabARIA, a human-supervised multi-agent framework that coordinates laboratory data, quality management, workflow optimization, and operational intelligence. By integrating specialized agents under transparent governance, LabARIA enables proactive laboratory management while preserving human oversight. Laboratory medicine offers a promising environment for developing, evaluating, and translating trustworthy agentic AI into healthcare delivery.

papers.title: When Does Context Compaction Pay in Long-Horizon Agents?
papers.summary: Abstract Context compaction replaces history with summaries, paying for their generation and changing an agent’s subsequent work. We study when this exchange pays on nine long Terminal-Bench tasks, continuing agents from common saved states to termination under repeated compaction, and check the results with complete runs and GPU replays. Holding the realized request sequence of synchronous compaction (Sync) fixed, compaction would have saved gpt-6.1-sol USD 0.17 per state at 64K and was favored at 18 of 21 states; continued to termination, Sync instead cost USD 0.26 more with measured cache reads, more at 20 of the 21. It added requests, mostly read-only, at all 48 saved states; the excess persisted with a continue cue, with Codex’s summary prompt, on four of five further tasks, and in the Codex CLI with its own compaction. In our runtime’s complete runs, with observed requests and cache allocations fixed, Sol’s Sync becomes cheaper only above a cache-read price of 34% of uncached input (16–87%; listed 5%); GLM’s crosses at 0.5% (listed 20%). Price alone does not explain the split: at one common price vector, compaction paid only where much work remained after the switch. On one GPU, compaction made a fixed-work pair of sessions 19% faster by avoiding a full KV pool; in a separate replay of two whole continuations, summary generation and added requests made Sync take 1.8 times

papers.title: Digital-Twin-Driven Predictive Maintenance and Fault-Tolerant Control for Electrified Agricultural Machinery: A Multiphysics and Deep Reinforcement Learning Framework for PMSM In-Wheel Drives
papers.summary: Electrified agricultural machinery increasingly relies on permanent-magnet synchronous motor drives that must remain dependable under variable traction, terrain-induced vibration, thermal cycling, contamination, and intermittent duty. Existing work offers mature methods for motor fault diagnosis, digital twins, predictive maintenance, and distributed-drive fault-tolerant control, but their health information is often not shared across diagnosis, maintenance, and control. This article develops a multiphysics digital-twin framework in which electrical, thermal, mechanical, and vibrational evidence maintains a probabilistic health belief that constrains both supervisory maintenance decisions and torque redistribution. The framework formalizes observability, uncertainty-aware health factors, deterministic safety shielding, multi-rate fallback logic, and agriculture-specific traction constraints. Reproducible low-fidelity numerical studies provide preliminary support for context-conditioned residual diagnosis and the revised thermal-continuity trade-off underlying health-aware derating, including robustness and sensitivity analyses. They do not validate sim-to-real transfer or the reinforcement-learning policy itself; those hypotheses remain open for dynamometer and hardware-in-the-loop testing. The results are therefore interpreted as mechanism-level evidence rather than field-perf

papers.title: Exploring or Exploiting Generative AI? A Dual-Path, Dual-Horizon Theory of Employee Incremental and Radical Creativity
papers.summary: Recent research has established that generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is not a unitary workplace resource: exploratory and exploitative use orientations are associated with different forms of employee creativity, and their value depends on employees' capacity to integrate generated knowledge. This article therefore does not present the basic dual path as a new discovery. Instead, it develops a theoretical integration and dynamic extension that asks why the established paths operate differently, when employees should switch between them, and how short-run augmentation can evolve into either capability accumulation or capability substitution. We distinguish expansive and consolidative modes of knowledge integration, theorize phase-congruent switching rather than static ``high-high'' ambidexterity, and position metacognition as a control mechanism that governs both immediate knowledge conversion and longer-run cognitive development. We further specify cultural tightness and psychological safety as directional boundary conditions and distinguish individual creative gains from collective idea-space diversity. The framework converts emerging empirical regularities into falsifiable propositions about task phase, context, and time, providing a research agenda for sustainable human--AI creativity.

papers.title: Designing and Explaining an Entrepreneurship Model for Artificial Intelligence–Based Businesses
papers.summary: The primary objective of the present study was to design and explain an entrepreneurship model for artificial intelligence–based businesses, with a focus on the information and communications technology and computer software industries in knowledge-based companies located in Tehran Province. In terms of purpose, the study was applied, and in terms of approach, it was a qualitative study employing a sequential exploratory design. In the qualitative phase, grounded theory was applied using the systematic approach to identify and conceptualize the dimensions, components, and relationships among the variables affecting AI-based entrepreneurship. The qualitative research field consisted of senior and middle managers, specialists, experts, and experienced employees working in the information and communications technology and computer software industries of knowledge-based companies in Tehran Province. Participants were selected through purposive sampling, which continued until theoretical saturation was reached. Qualitative data were collected through semi-structured interviews and analyzed using MAXQDA 2024. To enhance the credibility and trustworthiness of the data, triangulation and Lincoln and Guba’s criteria, including credibility, transferability, dependability, and confirmability, were employed. The findings indicated that the entrepreneurship model for AI-based businesses con

papers.title: GENERATIVE AI AND THE RESHAPING OF SECOND LANGUAGE WRITING: A COGNITIVE PROCESS PERSPECTIVE
papers.summary: Addressing how Generative AI (GenAI) reshapes the cognitive act of second language (L2) writing, this conceptual article draws on recent empirical literature (2023–2026). It grounds its analysis in the Cognitive Process Theory of Writing (CPTW), chosen because its decomposition of planning, translating, and reviewing under working-memory limits illuminates how cognitive labor is redistributed between learner and machine. Through CPTW, three key insights emerge. First, planning undergoes an externalization of productive struggle: offloading idea generation causes learners to bypass essential rhetorical problem framing. Second, translating experiences a voice constraint: model optimization toward conventionality flattens non-standard L2 syntax and homogenizes authorial voice. Third, reviewing suffers a reviewing bifurcation, splitting evaluation into goal-level appraisal and opaque decision-level monitoring. Theoretically, GenAI transforms writing into a co-generative sociotechnical practice requiring GenAI feedback literacy. Pedagogically, educators should adopt process-oriented assessments, using pre-prompting framing logs, annotated drafts, and prompt histories to evaluate cognitive engagement over polished final products.

papers.title: Citation Receipts: Auditing Retrieval-Backed Citation Events in Digital Libraries
papers.summary: Abstract Purpose: AI-assisted discovery can present a scholarly citation without leaving a publisher-verifiable event record. We study how digital libraries can audit one narrow class of source use: visible citations backed by authenticated retrieval. Methods: The Citation Receipt Protocol signs versioned source and response bindings, commits epoch sets to a Merkle log and audits sampled omissions. We separate provider declarations, client observations and publisher delivery. Evaluation includes controlled selective suppression, audit recognition, withholding, inflation, current-schema benchmarks, two distinct live-model studies and a saved-output suppression replay. Results: The preserved 300-call post-cutoff study produced 190 eligible receipts, all verified. A fresh 60-call context-intervention study produced 20 verified receipts in local replay with the target available and none when it was excluded or context was empty. A local replay of twenty saved answers detected two deliberate receipt omissions, with no false alarms. Selective-suppression experiments exposed the difference between pooled and publisher-conditioned sampling. Recognized probes passed despite omissions in organic traffic; valid committed receipts could still be withheld or fabricated. The current fixture measured a 935-byte payload and a 1,171-byte signed envelope. Conclusion: CRP supplies auditable prove

papers.title: Metacognitive disengagement and knowledge innovation quality in human–AI collaboration: the mediating role of cognitive offloading and the moderating roles of task complexity and AI literacy
papers.summary: Generative artificial intelligence is fundamentally reshaping the cognitive conditions of knowledge innovation. While human–AI collaboration improves the efficiency of knowledge production, it may also induce creators to outsourcing cognitive work to AI systems. This study conceptualized this tendency as task-level metacognitive disengagement, defined as the immediate reduction of planning, monitoring, and reflection within a specific AI-assisted task, and, drawing on metacognition theory, cognitive offloading theory and self-regulated learning theory, examined its impact on knowledge innovation quality, its psychological mechanism, and boundary conditions through four complementary experiments. Experiment 1 showed that higher AI assistance significantly increased metacognitive disengagement. Experiment 2 revealed that cognitive offloading partially mediated the relationship between AI assistance and metacognitive disengagement. Experiment 3 confirmed the negative effect of cognitive offloading on knowledge innovation quality, specifically on novelty, usefulness, and developability, with metacognitive disengagement partially mediating this effect. Experiment 4 tested the proposed moderated mediation model and found that task complexity strengthened, whereas individual AI literacy weakened, the negative indirect effect of cognitive offloading on knowledge innovation quality thro

papers.title: Video and digital games: Historical controversies, benefits, and risks for children and adolescents
papers.summary: Video and digital games have been the focus of sustained public and scientific debate since their commercial emergence in the late 1970s, particularly regarding their effects on children and adolescents. Early public and scientific discourse frequently portrayed gaming as a source of physical injury, addiction, aggression, social isolation, academic problems, and moral decline. However, subsequent empirical research has produced a substantially more differentiated picture of both the benefits and risks of gaming. This review examines the historical foundations of controversies surrounding video and digital games and synthesizes contemporary evidence concerning their cognitive, emotional, social, therapeutic, and physical effects. . Research indicates that moderate, purposeful gaming may improve visuospatial abilities, attentional control, problem-solving, mood regulation, social connection, and selected educational outcomes. Gaming-based interventions have also demonstrated therapeutic potential, particularly for depressive symptoms and attention-related difficulties among young people. At the same time, important risks remain, especially when gaming becomes excessive, compulsive, or disruptive to everyday functioning. These include repetitive-strain injuries, sleep disruption, problematic gaming, and adverse mental-health and academic outcomes. Evidence concerning violent game

papers.title: Designing a Curriculum Model Based on Artificial Intelligence and Purposeful Physical Activity to Enhance Learning Self-Regulation, Mental Health, and Psychological Well-Being among Students
papers.summary: Objective: The objective of this study was to design and validate a curriculum model based on artificial intelligence and purposeful physical activity with emphasis on enhancing learning self-regulation, mental health, and psychological well-being among students. Methods and Materials: This applied developmental study was conducted using an exploratory sequential mixed-methods design. In the qualitative phase, 20 experts in curriculum studies, educational technology, artificial intelligence in education, physical education, educational psychology, and student mental health were selected through purposive criterion-based sampling from Tehran and participated in semi-structured interviews. The interview data were analyzed using thematic analysis to extract the main dimensions, components, and indicators of the proposed curriculum model. In the quantitative phase, 384 secondary school students from Tehran were selected through multistage cluster sampling during the 2025–2026 academic year. Data were collected using a researcher-made curriculum model validation questionnaire, a learning self-regulation questionnaire, the General Health Questionnaire, and a psychological well-being scale. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, confirmatory factor analysis, and structural equation modeling. Findings: The inferential findings showed that the final curri

papers.title: Simulating Public Transit Fare Policies in NYC: An Efficient, Socioeconomic-Aware Framework
papers.summary: Designing equitable and effective public transit fare policies is challenging due to complex interactions among traveler behavior, multimodal networks, and socioeconomic heterogeneity. This paper presents a scalable, data-driven simulation framework for evaluating transit fare policies in New York City (NYC), integrating a synthetic population, agent-based simulation, multimodal travel-time estimation, and fare-sensitive mode choice modeling. We evaluate multiple fare scenarios, including distance-based pricing, fare increases, and fare-free bus policies. Results show that pricing changes modestly affect total ridership but significantly alter modal composition and produce heterogeneous impacts across income groups. In particular, fare-free bus policies generate substantial benefits for lower-income riders by increasing bus usage and reducing fare burden, while introducing trade-offs in revenue. To support city-scale analysis, we introduce a sampling-based approach that reduces computational cost while preserving aggregate accuracy. The proposed framework provides a practical tool for assessing trade-offs between ridership, revenue, and equity, enabling more informed and equitable transit policy design.

papers.title: Estuary and Ecofantasy: The Everyday Lives of Nipa Palm between Builder and Botanist
papers.summary: Abstract This text follows a well-known botanist along the shoreline of a Philippine island as he takes photographs of nipa palm ( nypa fruticans ), in its passage from plant to building part. It is January 1940 and David Fairchild is interested in plants for the collection of his new botanical garden in Miami, nicknamed ‘the kampong’. He takes a photograph of nipa being woven into roof shingles by women sitting cross-legged, watched by children. At the lens of Fairchild’s camera, the material forms of two world orders converge. One is the process of building construction in archipelagic Southeast Asia, a gendered process of manual fabrication where muscle-memory guides the way and instruction is by observation. The second is that of the camera, that tool of observation, tracking, and extracting of tropical environments. The article discusses the agency of these women in the context of the history of everyday labour forms that are systematically overlooked in architectural history, showing instead how the process is crucial to a contemporary body politics of the South and European perceptions of the tropics.

papers.title: Revisiting Conventional Models of Electoral Prediction: Insights from Nigeria's 2023 Presidential Election
papers.summary: Although electoral forecasting has received considerable scholarly attention, research systematically reassessing conventional prediction methods in relation to Nigeria’s electoral volatility, social media dynamics, and ethno-regional complexity remains limited. This study revisits opinion polls, historical voting patterns, and expert assessments in Nigeria’s 2023 presidential election and examines how social media sentiment can complement these approaches. A qualitative case study design was employed, drawing on eleven major pre-election polls, official results from the Independent National Electoral Commission, secondary sentiment-analysis datasets, and documentary sources. Comparative and thematic analyses were used to examine forecasting performance and identify methodological and contextual explanations for observed discrepancies. Conventional methods performed unevenly, with a reported failure rate of 63.6% among the eleven polling organisations reviewed. The analysis linked these shortcomings primarily to urban-centred sampling, inadequate turnout modelling, and insufficient attention to ethno-regional and religious cleavages. Approaches incorporating historical voting behaviour, turnout scenarios, and structural variables demonstrated greater predictive accuracy. Twitter sentiment provided timely indications of electoral competitiveness, although its contribution depend

papers.title: Integrative systems biology identifies shared neuroimmune co-expression programmes across pulmonary tuberculosis and Alzheimer's disease
papers.summary: Abstract Background : There is growing evidence that pulmonary tuberculosis (PTB) exerts long-lasting systemic effects on brain function, whereas Alzheimer's disease (AD) is increasingly recognized as a systemic neuroimmune disorder. BCG vaccination studies suggest that tuberculosis-associated immune pathways influence AD-related biology. However, whether PTB-associated co-expression programmes exhibit concordant activity in AD and display reproducible neuroanatomical organization within the human brain remains unknown. We hypothesized that PTB-associated co-expression programmes would exhibit concordant transcriptional activity in AD, retain aspects of their underlying co-expression architecture across diseases, and identify shared neuroimmune mechanisms relevant to chronic infection and neurodegeneration. We implemented an integrative systems biology framework combining whole-blood transcriptomics, weighted gene co-expression network analysis, functional enrichment, immune-cell deconvolution, and machine learning to identify PTB-associated co-expression programmes and prioritize biomarkers. These programmes were validated in two independent PTB cohorts, evaluated in an AD dataset, and mapped onto the Allen Human Brain Atlas to characterize neuroanatomical organization. Results: Active PTB was associated with widespread transcriptional remodeling, with 1,389 dysregulated genes

papers.title: Who Decides What to Measure? Social Entrepreneurs’ Ethical Decision-Making Dilemmas in the New Era of Mandatory Sustainability Reporting
papers.summary: Mandatory sustainability reporting is reshaping how organizations measure and communicate their impact, and its influence is no longer limited to large corporations. Emerging regulatory frameworks and standardized metrics are expected to trickle down into the world of social entrepreneurship, a field historically grounded in impact-driven values, context-specific outcomes, and normative commitments to inclusion, justice, and systemic change. In this commentary, we argue that the rise of mandatory sustainability reporting generates ethical dilemmas for social entrepreneurs as they navigate tensions between external reporting requirements and their normative commitments. We identify five interrelated ethical dilemmas related to ideology, identity, mission, resourcing, and collaboration, and examine how they unfold across four stages of ethical decision-making: moral awareness, moral judgment, moral intent, and moral behavior. In doing so, we offer a “thick conceptualization” of mandatory sustainability reporting as a moral issue that renders accountability decisions ethically consequential for social entrepreneurs and outline the resulting avenues for future research.

papers.title: The Age of AI Strategic Decision-Making: The Business Analytics in the Corporate Divisions as the Competitive Advantage
papers.summary: Abstract This paper examines how artificial intelligence (AI) and business analytics can be used strategically to improve corporate decision-making and create a sustainable competitive advantage in all key organizational processes. With data sets continuing to grow and market conditions growing more unpredictable, companies must shift past the management of their businesses by hunch and move to analytics-based and analytics-enabled strategic systems. Based on a qualitative, exploratory research design based on a systematic review of academic literature, industry reports, and practitioner case evidence published mainly within the past decade, the research investigates the use of AI-powered analytics in the fields of marketing, finance, human resources, and operations. The analysis summarizes the findings on how machine learning, predictive and prescriptive analytics, and real-time data processing can enhance the quality, speed, and agility of decisions for an organization. The results indicate that, although AI use has advanced quickly at the functional level, its strategic importance is often compromised by siloed use, legacy limitations, data quality issues, skills, and the inability to realize the benefits of the investment. papers.title: Process visualization feedback in news translation: a controlled intervention study of human-AI interaction using multimodal process data
papers.summary: Introduction This study examines process visualization feedback in news translation. Methods Framed within Krings' three-dimensional model, a pretest-posttest control group design was employed with 24 MTI students. The final analytic sample comprised 22 participants (11 experimental, 11 control). The experimental group ( n = 11) received personalized process visualizations and structured reflection; the control group ( n = 11) received conventional product-oriented feedback. Translation scores were available for both groups at T1 and T2, and complete process data (Inputlog, screen recording) were available for the experimental group at both time points. Results Within the experimental group, within-subject comparisons showed changes in all three dimensions: in the temporal dimension, increased pause time proportion indicated heightened metacognitive engagement ( p = 0.011); in the technical dimension, the meaning-level revision ratio increased significantly from 18.1% to 28.4% ( p = 0.002), indicating a shift from surface-level correction to deeper substantive refinement; in the cognitive dimension, participants made more strategic use of external sources, with significant increases in search engine queries ( p = 0.02) and knowledge-based searches ( p = 0.01).
